title: Websites that outlast us: dependency minimalism and the walkaway test applied to the frontend stack
description:
Walletbeat’s stack decisions treat browser-native behavior as a transfer of responsibility: shift implementation away from frameworks toward shared platform primitives, and accept progressive enhancement as an interim tradeoff for newer capabilities. Compilers sidestep the traditional server-client runtime model: Svelte bridges missing state, Astro produces static files, and subresource integrity ensures output is self-consistent.

Publication is designed around recovery: reject wallet-controlled services whose email recovery restores unilateral control, build once, then send artifacts through independent storage paths and checked browser access before updating ENS. IPFS content addresses are rollback targets, not promises of retention; ENS keeps automated updates revocable without granting ownership of the name. Conventional static hosts (Vercel, Cloudflare) remain the baseline; extra machinery earns its place only when it adds a verifiable or recoverable property the project values.
abstract: Walletbeat asks wallets to embody Ethereum values, so its maintainers turned the same scrutiny on the website that publishes its ratings. In a world of ossified consensus around "good enough" frontend stacks, what tradeoffs are still worth making? Using the site's static build pipeline as a case study, Darryl shows how principles of dependency minimalism and the walkaway test can help devs intentionally build resiliency, transparency and durability into web development and publishing workflows.
